holidays.name: Phileas Fogg Win a Wager Day
holidays.description: Pack your bags and your pocket watch. This day honors the famously punctual gentleman who circled the globe in 80 days and won a hefty bet. Celebrate by finishing something on a tight deadline, or by making a friendly wager of your own, perhaps about who can get the holiday shopping done fastest.
holidays.origin: It comes from Jules Verne's 1872 novel 'Around the World in Eighty Days'. Phileas Fogg believes he has lost his bet, but he actually gains a day by crossing the International Date Line. He reaches the Reform Club in London on December 21, just in time to win.
holidays.funFact: Fogg's trip was only believable because of new transport links in the 1870s, including the opening of the Suez Canal and new railways across India and the United States. Verne's story helped inspire real-life round-the-world races.

holidays.name: National French Fried Shrimp Day
holidays.description: Golden, crunchy, and ready for dipping. This day is a salute to shrimp that has been battered, breaded, and fried until crisp. Serve it with cocktail sauce, tartar sauce, or a squeeze of lemon, and call it a holiday feast.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It fits into the long tradition of days devoted to beloved fried foods.
holidays.funFact: Americans eat more shrimp than any other seafood, at roughly 4 to 5 pounds per person each year. That makes it the country's favorite catch by a wide margin.

holidays.name: Humbug Day
holidays.description: Today is a license to be grumpy about the holiday frenzy. Humbug Day invites you to channel your inner Ebenezer Scrooge, roll your eyes at the tinsel, and enjoy a short break from forced cheer. Then you can return to the season with a fresh attitude.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It takes its name from Scrooge's famous grumbling catchphrase in Charles Dickens's 1843 novella 'A Christmas Carol'.
holidays.funFact: Before Dickens made it famous, 'humbug' was already 18th-century slang for a hoax or sham. The word's exact origin is still a mystery.
